title: Chef Arun Vijayan Decodes Kerala's Gentle Spice Philosophy at Kolkata Pop-Up
excerpt: A traditional Kerala cuisine pop-up at Fairfield by Marriott, Kolkata, showcases the state's lighter, milder approach to spices — and why it stands apart from the rest of South India.
body:
• Chef Arun Vijayan is hosting a Taste of Kerala pop-up at Fairfield by Marriott, Kolkata, serving traditional recipes without any fusion modifications.
  • Kerala cuisine uses milder spices compared to Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, reflecting local preferences for lighter, less fiery dishes.
  • The pop-up features banana-leaf service, signature dishes like Pineapple Fish Moilee and Meen Manga Curry, and traditional dining customs including folding the leaf toward you to signal a satiated stomach.
  • Standout dishes include Chutta Kozhi Chaps, Kerala Chicken Roast, Pulissery, Kallappam, and Vendakka Mezhukkupuratti, with particular depth in seafood preparations.

Traditional Recipes, No Fusion

When Chef Arun Vijayan set up his Kerala cuisine pop-up at Fairfield by Marriott in Kolkata, he made a deliberate choice: no fusion, no shortcuts, no compromises on tradition.

"The reason to host this Kerala menu is because in Kolkata, people are expecting local and traditional food," Vijayan told Indulge Express. "We are not doing a fusion menu, and, in fact, we are keeping the traditional recipe intact and following it."

The result is a dinner service that functions as much as a cultural education as a meal. Earthen bowls with warm water for hand-washing arrive first. Then come long banana leaves — the traditional plates of South Indian households — neatly marked so diners can fold them in either direction. When the meal is done, folding the leaf toward you signals appreciation and a satisfied appetite.

Why Kerala Spices Are Different

Kerala is famous as the land of spices — pepper, cardamom, cloves, and cinnamon all trace their origins to the state's Western Ghats. Yet the paradox of Kerala cuisine is that despite this abundance, the food is remarkably gentle compared to its South Indian neighbors.

"In Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, they use strong spices. But in Kerala, we use mild spices only. The difference is because of people's expectations. In Kerala, people don't like to have a lot of spicy dishes."

— Chef Arun Vijayan

This distinction sets Kerala apart in the South Indian culinary landscape. Where Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu lean into heat and intensity, Kerala favors coconut milk, curry leaves, and tamarind to build flavor with subtlety. The cooking lets individual ingredients speak rather than competing for attention.

What to Order

The Indulge Express review highlights a menu built on depth rather than spectacle. The Pineapple Fish Moilee stands out — a coconut-based fish curry where the tropical sweetness of pineapple plays against the gentle heat of the gravy. The Meen Manga Curry brings raw mango into the equation, adding the sour tang that defines Kerala's coastal cooking.

Fish lovers get ample choices across the menu, but the non-seafood dishes hold their own. The Chutta Kozhi Chaps and Kerala Chicken Roast showcase the state's approach to poultry — aromatic rather than fiery, with slow-built spice layers. The Pulissery, a yogurt-based curry, offers a cooling counterpoint.

The Kallappam — lacy, fermented rice pancakes — and Vendakka Mezhukkupuratti, a dry okra stir-fry seasoned with curry leaves and red chilies, round out the experience with everyday Kerala home cooking elevated for the pop-up format.

Kerala's Food Story for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, Kerala cuisine often gets reduced to a handful of greatest hits — appam and stew, fish curry and rice, beef fry for the adventurous. Vijayan's pop-up pushes beyond that familiar territory into the quieter corners of the state's culinary tradition, where the food is lighter than most diners expect and the spice philosophy is more about restraint than firepower.

The pop-up runs for lunch and dinner service at Fairfield by Marriott, Kolkata.
